newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania poll foes draw thousands to last rallies.
newsitem.headline: Romania poll foes draw thousands to last rallies.

text.p: Thousands of Romanians marched through the streets of Bucharest on Thursday as front-runner President Ion Iliescu and his main opponent brought a bitter general election campaign to an end.
"We want a new term in office in order to build on what we have started to build," Iliescu, in power since the fall of communism in 1989, told about 8,000 supporters.

More than twice that number were led in a rival march by Emil Constantinescu of the Democratic Convention bloc (CDR) past buildings still pock-marked by bullet holes from the violent revolt which ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

Campaigning ends 48 hours before Sunday's vote. The finale is a marathon late-night television debate on Thursday between all 16 presidential hopefuls, including a faith healer, a retired general and the leader of a car owners' party.
Opinion polls show Constantinescu closing the gap in the home stretch, only four points behind Iliescu's 32 percent.
Former prime minister Petre Roman is third on 21 percent. A run-off round is almost certain to follow in mid-November.
Surrounded by his campaign staff, top ministers and several dozen teenage girls waving blue-and-white pom poms, Iliescu said: "Our rivals want to set back the wheel of history."
"That is why we must win the elections, to protect the country from more suffering," he told supporters, many waving blue flags of his leftwing Party of Social Democracy (PDSR).

Police lined thoroughfares in the city centre for the opposition march, which passed off without incident. Thousands of leaflets attacking Constantinescu fluttered onto the streets from a light plane overhead.
"Down with Iliescu...No more Bolshevik president," shouted the marchers, jeering as they walked past PDSR headquarters.
"Dreams will come true!" Constantinescu shouted in Revolution Square, where Ceausescu fled by helicopter on December 22, 1989 before being captured and executed at an army barracks on Christmas Day.
"Like millions of others, your dream is to change Romania's destiny," said Constantinescu, who was thrashed by Iliescu in a presidential run-off four years ago.
As well as choosing a president voters face a confusing field of some 15 parties vying for seats in both houses of parliament in the country's third post-communist polls.

Latest opinion surveys suggest a large turnout on Sunday, which would help Iliescu's chances. His PDSR trails Constantinescu's CDR in the parliamentary poll, likely to be followed by tough bargaining over coalition partners.
"The Romanian political establishment faces a major democratic test on Sunday -- a transfer of power," the independent newspaper Adevarul said in an editorial.
"Romania is the only East European country where there has been no real transfer of power since the fall of communism."
The six-week campaign has abounded in muck-racking, with vicious attacks from all sides, mainly on television.
The PDSR portrays Constantinescu as a closet monarchist, -- a damning charge in a country with now solid republican roots.

"Emil Constantinescu promised that he would surrender power to the former king when he becomes president," said PDSR executive leader Adrian Nastase. Supporters duly booed the absent bearded academic.
